title: Environment and Sustainable Development
summary: The environment supplies resources, absorbs waste and sustains life, but economic growth has pushed its use beyond its carrying capacity. This chapter explains the functions of the environment, the environmental crisis, India's environmental challenges and the strategies for sustainable development.

notes.heading: Environment and its four functions
notes.html:
Environment is the total planetary inheritance and the totality of all resources. It includes biotic elements (plants, animals, birds, forests, fisheries) and abiotic elements (air, water, land, sunlight, rocks).

  1. Supplies resources: renewable (trees, fish, water) and non-renewable (coal, petroleum, minerals).
  2. Assimilates waste generated by production and consumption.
  3. Sustains life by providing genetic and biodiversity.
  4. Provides aesthetic services such as scenery and recreation.

notes.heading: Carrying capacity, absorptive capacity and the crisis
notes.html:
• The environment performs its functions without interruption only if demand stays within its carrying capacity: resource extraction must not exceed the rate of regeneration, and waste must not exceed the absorptive capacity (the ability to absorb degradation).
  • When these limits are crossed there is an environmental crisis: resources are depleted and pollution builds up.
  • Reasons: rising population, affluent consumption and production standards of the developed world, intensive extraction of renewable and non-renewable resources, industrialisation and urbanisation.

Reversal of supply and demand

Before industrialisation, demand for environmental resources and services was much less than their supply. Now demand exceeds supply, so environmental quality itself has become scarce.

Opportunity cost of negative environmental impact

Polluted air and water raise spending on health; depleted resources force huge expenditure on research to find substitutes and on restoring quality. These costs are the opportunity cost of environmental damage.

notes.heading: Global warming and ozone depletion
notes.html:
BasisGlobal warmingOzone depletion
MeaningGradual rise in the average temperature of the earth's lower atmosphereReduction in the amount of ozone in the stratosphere
CauseGreenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane) from burning fossil fuels and deforestationChlorine and bromine compounds: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used in air-conditioners and refrigerators, halons in fire extinguishers
EffectsMelting polar ice, rising sea level, coastal flooding, extinction of species, more tropical storms and diseasesMore ultraviolet radiation reaching the earth: skin cancer, lower production of phytoplankton, harm to aquatic life and plant growth
Global responseKyoto Protocol (1997) and later climate agreementsMontreal Protocol banning CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals

notes.heading: State of India's environment
notes.html:
India is rich in natural resources: fertile black soil of the Deccan, the Indo-Gangetic plains, forests, and mineral deposits of iron ore, coal and natural gas. Yet development has put heavy pressure on them.

Dichotomy of threat: India faces poverty-induced degradation (e.g. cutting forests for fuel) and, at the same time, pollution from affluence and rapid industrial growth.

Major concerns

  • Land degradation: caused by loss of vegetation through deforestation, unsustainable fuelwood and fodder extraction, shifting cultivation, encroachment into forest land, forest fires and overgrazing, improper crop rotation, indiscriminate use of fertilisers and pesticides, poor irrigation management, and over-extraction of groundwater.
  • Biodiversity loss.
  • Air pollution, especially vehicular pollution in urban areas.
  • Management of fresh water and solid waste.

India supports a large share of the world's human and cattle population on a small share of its land area, so pressure on land is intense.

Pollution control boards

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) was set up in 1974 to address water and air pollution, followed by State boards. They investigate and collect information on pollution, lay down standards for sewage and industrial effluents, give technical assistance to governments, and conduct research and awareness programmes.

notes.heading: Sustainable development
notes.html:
Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (UNCED; popularised by the Brundtland Commission report, 'Our Common Future').

  • It asks the present generation to leave the future generation a stock of 'quality of life' assets no less than what it inherited.
  • It stresses meeting the basic needs of all, especially the poor, and equitable distribution.

Herman Daly's conditions

  • Limit the human population to a level within the carrying capacity.
  • Technological progress should be input-efficient, not input-consuming.
  • Renewable resources should be extracted on a sustainable basis (extraction ≤ regeneration).
  • Depletion of non-renewable resources should not exceed the rate of creation of renewable substitutes.
  • Inefficiencies arising from pollution should be corrected.

notes.heading: Strategies for sustainable development
notes.html:
• Non-conventional sources of energy: wind and solar power instead of thermal and hydro power, which have adverse environmental effects.
  • LPG and gobar gas in rural areas: replace wood, dung cakes and biomass, reducing deforestation and indoor air pollution.
  • CNG in urban areas: use of compressed natural gas in public transport has lowered air pollution, as in Delhi.
  • Wind power: windmills in high-wind areas generate electricity without pollution.
  • Solar power through photovoltaic cells: free of pollution and useful for remote areas.
  • Mini-hydel plants: use perennial mountain streams to run small turbines for local needs without changing land use.
  • Traditional knowledge and practices: Ayurveda, Unani, Tibetan and folk systems, which are environment-friendly.
  • Bio-composting: organic manure and earthworm-based (vermi) compost in place of chemical fertilisers.
  • Bio-pest control: neem-based pesticides, mixed cropping, and awareness that snakes, owls and peacocks control pests naturally.

keyTerms.definition: The total planetary inheritance and the totality of all resources, including biotic and abiotic factors.
The limit up to which the environment can supply resources and absorb waste without damage.
The ability of the environment to absorb degradation.
Resources that can be used without the possibility of exhaustion because they are replenished, such as trees and fish.
Resources that get exhausted with extraction and use, such as fossil fuels.
A gradual increase in the average temperature of the earth's lower atmosphere due to greenhouse gases.
Reduction in the amount of ozone in the stratosphere, caused mainly by CFCs.
Development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
Decline in the overall quality of soil, water or vegetation caused by human activities or nature.

mcqs.explanation: Abiotic elements are non-living: air, water, land and sunlight.

options: Use of CNG in public transport
Greater use of thermal power plants
mcqs.explanation: Thermal power plants emit large quantities of greenhouse gases and fly ash.

mcqs.explanation: Sustainable development covers both meeting the basic needs of the present, especially of the poor, and protecting the future.

mcqs.explanation: The reversal of the supply-demand relationship after industrialisation is what makes environmental quality scarce.

questions.q: What is meant by the carrying capacity of the environment?
questions.answerHtml: It means that resource extraction is not above the rate of regeneration of the resource, and the waste generated is within the absorptive capacity of the environment.

questions.q: Explain how the opportunity cost of negative environmental impacts is high.
questions.answerHtml:
• Health costs: decline in air and water quality increases respiratory and water-borne diseases, raising expenditure on health.
  • Cost of substitutes: exhaustion of resources forces heavy spending on research and technology to explore new resources.
  • Cost of restoration: global issues such as global warming and ozone depletion require large financial commitments from governments.

These resources could have been used for other development purposes; hence the opportunity cost is high.

questions.q: 'India's environmental problems pose a dichotomy.' Explain.
questions.answerHtml:
India faces two opposite sources of environmental threat at the same time:

  • Poverty-induced degradation: the poor depend directly on nature and over-use it, e.g. cutting trees for fuelwood, overgrazing, cultivating marginal land.
  • Affluence-induced pollution: rapidly growing industry, vehicles and high consumption in cities cause air and water pollution and waste.

So both under-development and development damage the environment.

questions.q: Explain any four functions of the environment.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Supplies resources: it provides renewable and non-renewable resources used as inputs for production.
  2. Assimilates waste: it absorbs the waste generated by production and consumption.
  3. Sustains life: it provides the genetic and biodiversity essential for life.
  4. Provides aesthetic services: scenery such as mountains, rivers and forests improves the quality of life.

questions.q: What is sustainable development? Explain any four strategies to achieve it in India.
questions.answerHtml:
Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

  1. Non-conventional energy: wind and solar energy are cleaner than thermal and large hydro plants.
  2. LPG and gobar gas in rural areas: they replace firewood and dung cakes, reducing deforestation and household air pollution.
  3. CNG in urban areas: using CNG in public transport lowers vehicular air pollution.
  4. Bio-composting and bio-pest control: organic manure, vermicompost and neem-based pesticides replace chemicals that harm soil and water.

Together these reduce pressure on non-renewable resources and keep pollution within the absorptive capacity of the environment.
